newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Central bankers to brief G10 on supervision.
newsitem.headline: Central bankers to brief G10 on supervision.

text.p: Central bank governors from the Group of 10 (G10) leading industrial nations will brief their finance ministers on progress made in tightening cooperation among supervisors of the banking, insurance and securities industries, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Monday.

Tietmeyer, speaking as chairman of the G10 central bank governors' committee, told reporters at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) that he would give G10 ministers an overview of the work done by the three groups of supervisors.
Tietmeyer's briefing is based on a report that was delivered to G10 central bankers on Monday by Tommaso Padoa-Schioppa, chairman of the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision.

Padoa-Schioppa gave the G10 an overview of the supervisory work done in risk management and transparency, and the cooperation between the Basle Committee, the International Organisation of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) and the International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS).
"The question of cooperation among supervisors is becoming more and more important and we will inform the ministers of where we stand," Tietmeyer said.

At their Lyon summit last June, the Group of Seven (G7) industrial powers agreed that one of its objectives for the next year was to increase cooperation among authorities supervising internationally active financial institutions.
Banking sources have said the G10 would give G7 ministers an interim report about the work of supervisors at the G7 meeting in Berlin on February 8.
Cooperation among the supervisors of the three branches of the financial industry is taking place in the Joint Forum on Financial Conglomerates, chaired by Tom de Swaan of the Dutch central bank.

Banking, insurance and securities industry supervisors are tightening their cooperation to catch up with financial conglomerates, which now have activities that span across the entire range of financial services.

The collapse of British merchant bank Barings Plc in 1995 highlighted gaping holes in global supervision and a lack of cooperation between supervisors of individual institutions and regulators of exchanges.
